'''Robert K. McMahan''' (born 1961) is an American [[physicist]], [[Professors in the United States|professor]], and [[entrepreneur]] who is the seventh and current [[University president|president]] of [[Kettering University]].<ref name=KU>{{cite news|url=https://www.kettering.edu/news/new-president-named|title=New President Named|date=Jun 13, 2011|publisher=[[Kettering University]]}}</ref><ref name="UCSRecord">[http://www.gpo.gov/fdsys/pkg/CREC-2012-04-16/html/CREC-2012-04-16-pt1-PgE538-4.htm Congressional Record Volume 158, Number 54 (Monday, April 16, 2012).]</ref>

==Biography and career==
===Academic===
McMahan received undergraduate degrees in physics and the history of art from [[Duke University]] in 1982 and a Ph.D. in physics from [[Dartmouth College|Dartmouth]] in 1986 under [[Gary A. Wegner|Gary Wegner]]. After a postdoctoral appointment at the [[Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics|Center for Astrophysics {{!}} Harvard & Smithsonian]] under [[Margaret Geller]] (1986-1989), and while also engaged in a number of corporate and public sector roles (see ''Corporate and Public'' below), he served as a research professor of physics and astronomy at the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]] from 1989-2008<ref>{{cite web | last = Smith | first = Jason | title = A New Telescope Sets Its Sights on Blue Heaven|publisher = UNC Global, Endeavors Magazine|url = http://global.unc.edu/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=126&Itemid=104 |access-date = October 26, 2012}}</ref> as well as a visiting scholar at Oxford University and the University of Durham (UK). He joined [[Western Carolina University]] in 2008 as the founding dean of the Kimmel School and Professor of Engineering<ref name="WCUappoint">{{cite news|url=http://www.wcu.edu/6103.asp|title=State technology adviser McMahan appointed dean of Kimmel School|date=January 25, 2008|publisher=[[Western Carolina University]]}}</ref>  prior to becoming the seventh president of [[Kettering University]] in 2011, where he also holds an appointment as a tenured professor of physics.<ref name=KU/>

McMahan is known for computational modeling and observational work in [[white dwarf]] stars early in his career, then later for work in [[cosmology]] and [[extragalactic astronomy]].<ref name="adsabs.harvard.edu">[http://adsabs.harvard.edu/ads_abstracts.html SAO/NASA ADS at SAO: ADS Abstract Service]</ref> As a graduate student he was involved with the ''Seven Samurai'' research group that postulated the existence of the [[Great Attractor]].<ref>Dressler, Alan. ''Voyage to the Great Attractor: Exploring Intergalactic Space.''  New York, Alfred A. Knopf, 1994.</ref><ref>[[Donald Lynden-Bell]]</ref> This effort resulted in the development of a methodology of estimating the distance to galaxies which, when applied, has become one of the most reliable ways to measure the total mass density of the universe.  As a postdoc at the [[Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics|Center for Astrophysics {{!}} Harvard & Smithsonian]] under [[Margaret Geller]] he participated in research that resulted in the development of maps of the [[large-scale structure of the universe]], which led to the discovery of the [[CfA2 Great Wall|Great Wall]].
<ref>Frontline, Jan 1, 2010, "In 1989, Margaret Geller and John Huchra, on the basis of redshift survey data, discovered the presence of the Great (Galactic) Wall..."</ref>
<ref>{{cite news | url=https://pqasb.pqarchiver.com/washingtonpost/access/73911540.html?dids=73911540:73911540&FMT=ABS&FMTS=ABS:FT&type=current&date=Nov+18%2C+1989&author=William+Booth&pub=The+Washington+Post+(pre-1997+Fulltext)&desc=Vast+Sheet+of+Galaxies+Found+In+the+Far+Reaches+of+Space%3B%60Great+Wall%27+Largest+Structure+Detected+in+Universe&pqatl=google | first=William | last=Booth | title=Vast Sheet of Galaxies Found In the Far Reaches of Space;'Great Wall' Largest Structure Detected in Universe | date=November 18, 1989 | access-date=July 7, 2017 | archive-date=December 1, 2017 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171201182024/https://pqasb.pqarchiver.com/washingtonpost/doc/307210384.html?FMT=ABS&FMTS=ABS%3AFT&type=current&date=Nov%2018%2C%201989&author=William%20Booth&pub=The%20Washington%20Post%20%28pre-1997%20Fulltext%29&edition=&startpage=&desc=Vast%20Sheet%20of%20Galaxies%20Found%20In%20the%20Far%20Reaches%20of%20Space%3B%60Great%20Wall%27%20Largest%20Structure%20Detected%20in%20Universe | url-status=dead }}</ref>
<ref>Charles Choi. [http://sciencenow.sciencemag.org/cgi/content/citation/2003/1024/1 That Wall in China Is Nothing], ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'', 24 October 2003</ref>
<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7toILlSQtI0C&pg=PA214 |title=The Inflationary Universe: The Quest for a New Theory of Cosmic Origins - Alan H. Guth - Google Boeken |access-date=2012-05-22|isbn=9780201328400 |last1=Guth |first1=Alan |year=1997 |publisher=Basic Books }}</ref> 
<ref name="redshift">[http://www.sciencemag.org/cgi/content/abstract/246/4932/897 M. J. Geller & J. P. Huchra, ''Science'' '''246''', 897 (1989).]</ref>

He was a member of the EFAR project, a detailed study of the [[peculiar velocity]] distribution of a large number elliptical-rich [[Galaxy groups and clusters|galaxy clusters]].<ref name="adsabs.harvard.edu" /> At the [[Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics|Center for Astrophysics {{!}} Harvard & Smithsonian]] he developed 3D visualization software that was used in the 40-minute film, ''So Many Galaxies...So Little Time,'' which was on display at the [[National Air and Space Museum]].

He has published over 50 articles in astronomy and astrophysics, engineering and public policy and holds five US patents.<ref name="adsabs.harvard.edu" /><ref name="RKM">{{cite web | title = Biography | url = http://www.kettering.edu/president/biography | access-date = October 26, 2012 | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20121028163209/https://www.kettering.edu/president/biography | archive-date = October 28, 2012 }}</ref>

McMahan assumed the position of president of [[Kettering University]] on August 1, 2011.<ref name=KUPresidents>{{cite web | title = History of the Presidency | url = https://www.kettering.edu/president/archives/succession-presidents | access-date = October 26, 2012 | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20121028163009/https://www.kettering.edu/president/archives/succession-presidents | archive-date = October 28, 2012 }}</ref>

===Corporate and public===
While at the [[Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics|Center for Astrophysics {{!}} Harvard & Smithsonian]], McMahan founded McMahan Research Laboratories, an applied physics systems research and development firm in Cambridge, Massachusetts in 1988, which relocated to the [[Research Triangle Park]] of [[North Carolina]] in 1989 and later was acquired in 2000 by Gretag-Macbeth.<ref>Gretag–Macbeth, once a subsidiary of Kollmorgen, has subsequently gone through a series of mergers, reorganizations, and acquisitions. The name now belongs to [[Danaher Corporation]].</ref> He then joined [[In-Q-Tel]], a private venture capital organization funded by the CIA, and afterward served as the senior advisor to the governor of North Carolina for science and technology, and the executive director of the North Carolina Board of Science and Technology from 2003-2008<ref name="TBJprofile">[http://www.bizjournals.com/triad/stories/2006/07/03/newscolumn3.html?page=all Governor's senior adviser has his job down to a science. ''The Business Journal'' July 3, 2006.]</ref> where he led the development of significant state and national innovation, investment capital, and technology based economic development policies and legislation,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.ssti.org/Digest/2005/082905.htm |title=North Carolina Creates SBIR/STTR Incentive, Matching Program |access-date=2014-03-31 |archive-date=2012-08-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120808055857/http://www.ssti.org/Digest/2005/082905.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>''Triangle Business Journal.'' May 26, 2006</ref><ref>{{cite news | title = ''Tar Heel of the Week'' | newspaper = Raleigh News & Observer| date = October 19, 2003}}</ref> and was a frequent international speaker on academic entrepreneurship and on the role of universities in economic development.<ref>[http://www.nap.edu/openbook.php?record_id=12546&page=113 ''Understanding Research, Science and Technology Parks: Global Best Practice: Report of a Symposium.'' The National Academies Press (2009).]</ref><ref>[http://www.milkeninstitute.org/events/events.taf?function=show&cat=allconf&EventID=GC07&SPID=2548&level1=speakers&level2=bio&ID= Milken Institute Global Conference (2007).]</ref><ref>[http://www.nap.edu/openbook.php?record_id=12160&page=62 ''State Science and Technology Policy Advice: Issues, Opportunities, and Challenges: Summary of a National Convocation.'' The National Academies Press (2008).]</ref><ref>[http://www.clevelandfed.org/research/conferences/2006/november/bio.cfm The Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland (2006).]</ref>

==Personal==
McMahan has been married to the former Karen Deschamps, a graduate of [[McGill University]], since 1989. They have two children.
